newsitem.title: USA: Potato chip crunch time - spuds in short supply.
newsitem.headline: Potato chip crunch time - spuds in short supply.

text.p: Heavy rains wiped out half of Florida's potato crop three weeks ago and ever since potato chip makers have been scrambling to find the right spuds to make the crunchy snacks Americans crave.

"Anywhere from 30 to 50 percent of the crop was wiped out by the heavy rains," Florida Agriculture Department spokesman Terry McElroy said, noting the panhandle region received about 17 inches of rain in some areas.
Potatoes are a $100 million-a-year crop for Florida. The affected region was declared a disaster area, McElroy said.
The devastated crop meant headaches for companies such as Frito-Lay and the Cape Cod Chip Co., but was unlikely to lead to higher prices at the grocery store, company officials said.

"We did experience some shortages," said Lynn Markley, a spokeswoman for Frito-Lay, a unit of PepsiCo Inc. "But we've been able to get alternate supplies. Florida is not the only state that grows eastern whites. We're still able to get supply from Texas and Arizona."
Eastern whites, with their round fleshy meat, are preferred to other types of potatoes for making chips.
Nicole Bernard, a spokeswoman for Cape Cod Chip Co., said her family-owned business based in Hyannis, Mass., noticed the shortage of eastern whites immediately.
"Prices almost tripled for potatoes," she said. Chip makers reported paying 22 cents a pound, up from seven cents a pound. "We've been searching in North Carolina for the right supply."
Some chip makers have turned to other types of potatoes or bought older, stored crops, state agriculture officials said.

"The market has gotten pretty tight for eastern whites," said Maine Department of Agriculture spokesman John Logan. "Now, you're seeing the chip makers compete in the table potato market to get enough supply. It's the old law of supply and demand working."
But consumers will not see price increases, Frito-Lay and Cape Cod officials said.
"The consumer will not notice any difference -- in either taste or price," said Frito-Lay's Markley.
"It wouldn't be fair to pass on this type of expense to our customers," Cape Cod's Bernard said.

Bernard expects the shortage, which is concentrated along the eastern seaboard, to ease in about two weeks when crops further north start to be harvested. "Which means there will be plenty of potato chips available for July Fourth," she said.
Frito-Lay's Markley estimated the company will sell the equivalent of 76 million pounds of potatoes made into its Lay's and Ruffles brands of chips during the Independence Day weekend.
